blocks.text: 1. ML Pipelines
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504398-650799649.png

The Model Deployment module closed with Serialization through Retraining Strategies, covering one single model's full lifecycle from saving it to eventually retraining it. Production Machine Learning zooms out considerably further, to the full system and process surrounding many models running together in a real organization.

An ML Pipeline is the automated, ordered sequence of steps that turns raw data into a deployed, monitored model, without requiring a person to manually run each step by hand every single time. It is the foundational structure the rest of this module builds directly on top of.
2. Why Manual Steps Break Down
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504398-825497613.png

Running data cleaning, training, and evaluation as separate, manual notebook steps works fine for a single, one-off experiment, but it breaks down quickly once a model needs to be maintained over time. It becomes genuinely easy to forget a step entirely, or to run steps out of their correct order without noticing.

There is also typically no clear record of exactly which data and which code actually produced a given model, since manual steps rarely leave behind a precise, reliable trail. This makes the whole process essentially impossible to reliably repeat later, or to hand off cleanly to a different team member who was not present for the original manual run.
3. The Stages of a Typical Pipeline

blocks.alt: The Stages of a Typical Pipeline
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504399-852612696.png

A typical ML Pipeline begins with raw data ingestion, pulling in data from wherever it originates, followed by data validation and cleaning, catching obvious problems before they propagate further downstream. Feature engineering comes next, applying exactly the transformations already covered in that earlier module, consistently and automatically every single run.

Model training follows, then model evaluation, checked against the same established metrics covered throughout the Model Evaluation modules, and finally model registration and deployment, the subjects of upcoming topics in this module. Each stage's output feeds directly into the next stage's input, forming one continuous, automated flow.

blocks.text: 4. The DAG Concept
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504399-831920846.png

A pipeline is structured internally as a Directed Acyclic Graph, commonly abbreviated a DAG, where each individual stage is represented as a node, and each dependency between stages is represented as a directed edge pointing from one stage toward the stage that depends on it.

Acyclic specifically means no stage can ever depend on a later stage, only on earlier ones that have already completed, ruling out any circular dependency entirely. This DAG structure is what lets a pipeline orchestration tool automatically run genuinely independent stages in parallel, whenever the dependency graph actually allows it, rather than forcing every stage to run strictly one after another.
5. What Makes a Pipeline Genuinely Reproducible

blocks.alt: What Makes a Pipeline Genuinely Reproducible
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504399-765413261.png

A genuinely reproducible pipeline tracks the exact code version used for every single run, typically through version control, a specific Git commit hash for instance, pinning precisely which code actually produced a given model. It also tracks the exact data version used, an idea covered in considerably more depth in the upcoming Data Pipelines topic.

And it tracks the exact configuration and hyperparameters used for that particular run, a concern covered fully in Experiment Tracking, another upcoming topic in this module. Together, these three tracked elements mean any past model can, in principle, be recreated exactly, a genuinely valuable property whenever debugging a past problem or auditing a model's history.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Reproducibility is not just an academic nicety. It is what allows a team to confidently answer the question "why did this specific model behave this way" months after that model was actually trained.

blocks.text: 6. Common Orchestration Tools

Apache Airflow is a general-purpose workflow scheduling tool, widely used across data engineering more broadly, not exclusively for machine learning, making it a common choice in organizations that already rely on it elsewhere. Kubeflow Pipelines is built specifically for machine learning workflows running on Kubernetes, offering tighter integration with ML-specific concerns.

MLflow Pipelines, or even a simple custom script for smaller-scale projects, offer lighter-weight options that avoid the operational overhead of running a full orchestration platform, a genuinely reasonable choice when a project's scale does not yet justify heavier infrastructure.

blocks.text: 7. Handling Failures Within a Pipeline
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504898-474916629.png

A pipeline stage can genuinely fail partway through a run, training crashing on an unexpectedly bad batch of data for instance. A well-built pipeline retries transient failures automatically, a temporary network issue for example, without requiring a person to notice and manually restart the whole thing.

It also stops cleanly, with a clear, actionable error message, when a genuine, non-transient failure occurs, and it should never silently continue past a failed stage into the next one, since doing so risks producing a model built on incomplete or corrupted intermediate results without anyone realizing it happened.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A pipeline that silently continues past a failed stage, perhaps using stale or partial data from a previous successful run, is a genuinely dangerous failure mode, since it can produce a model that looks successfully trained while actually being built on broken input.

blocks.text: 8. Connecting to CI/CD for ML

This connects forward to CI/CD for ML, an upcoming topic later in this module. An ML Pipeline can itself be triggered automatically by a code change, a new commit to the feature engineering logic for instance, rather than requiring a person to manually kick off a new run.

This connects traditional software continuous integration and continuous deployment practices directly to the machine learning training process itself, treating a pipeline run as just another automated step in a broader, familiar software delivery workflow, rather than a separate, disconnected activity.
9. When a Formal Pipeline Genuinely Matters

blocks.alt: When a Formal Pipeline Genuinely Matters
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444504899-320636977.png

A formal ML Pipeline genuinely matters for any model that gets retrained more than once, ever, since manual, ad hoc retraining simply does not scale reliably beyond a first, one-time run, exactly the breakdown covered earlier in this topic.

It matters just as much whenever multiple team members work on the same model, a shared, automated pipeline removing any ambiguity about how the model actually gets built, rather than leaving that knowledge trapped in one person's head or one person's personal notebook.
10. Worked Example
The example below implements a minimal pipeline function that runs the core stages in sequence, with basic failure handling around each stage.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

def run_pipeline(raw_data, raw_labels):
    stages_completed = []

    try:
        clean_data = raw_data[~np.isnan(raw_data).any(axis=1)]
        clean_labels = raw_labels[~np.isnan(raw_data).any(axis=1)]
        stages_completed.append("validation_and_cleaning")

        features = np.hstack([clean_data, clean_data[:, [0]] * clean_data[:, [1]]])
        stages_completed.append("feature_engineering")

        model = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42)
        model.fit(features, clean_labels)
        stages_completed.append("training")

        predictions = model.predict(features)
        accuracy = accuracy_score(clean_labels, predictions)
        stages_completed.append("evaluation")

        if accuracy < 0.6:
            raise ValueError(f"Model accuracy {accuracy:.2f} below minimum threshold, stopping before deployment")

        print(f"Pipeline succeeded: stages completed = {stages_completed}")
        print(f"Training accuracy: {accuracy:.4f}")
        return model

    except Exception as error:
        print(f"Pipeline failed after stages: {stages_completed}")
        print(f"Error: {error}")
        return None

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
raw_data = rng.normal(size=(500, 3))
raw_labels = (raw_data[:, 0] + raw_data[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)
run_pipeline(raw_data, raw_labels)

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Notice the pipeline stops cleanly with a clear error if accuracy falls below a minimum threshold, rather than deploying a genuinely poor model automatically, exactly the disciplined failure handling covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: An ML Pipeline automates the full sequence from raw data to a deployed model.
Manual notebook steps are easy to forget or reorder, and leave no reliable record of what produced a given model.
A typical pipeline flows through ingestion, validation, feature engineering, training, evaluation, and deployment.
A pipeline is structured as a DAG, stages as nodes, dependencies as directed edges, no cycles allowed.
Genuine reproducibility requires tracking the exact code, data, and configuration used for every run.
Common orchestration tools include Apache Airflow, Kubeflow Pipelines, and lighter options for smaller projects.
A well-built pipeline retries transient failures but stops cleanly on genuine ones, never silently continuing past a failure.
A pipeline can be triggered automatically by a code change, connecting to CI/CD for ML, covered later in this module.
Next up: Data Pipelines, a closer look at the data-handling stages that feed into an ML Pipeline.
